title: Lunch specials ideas for restaurant takeout calls
seoTitle: Lunch specials ideas for restaurant takeout | ROAL
description: Use lunch specials that are easy to sell by phone, with simple combos, pricing tips, and faster pickup planning.
question: What lunch specials ideas restaurant owners can use to get more takeout calls?
answer: Use lunch specials that are easy to order by phone, fast to make, and clear to repeat back: a sandwich or slice combo, a plated lunch plate, a soup-and-half-sandwich deal, or a limited-time weekday special. Keep the names simple, prices easy to hear, and add-ons short so callers can place pickup orders without a long back-and-forth.
summary: Build lunch specials that are easy to order, easy to quote, and easy for your kitchen to make fast.
intro:
Lunch specials ideas restaurant owners can use for takeout calls should be simple, quick to make, and easy to quote on the phone. The best ones are the meals people already want at noon, packaged as a clear combo with one price and a fast ready time.

For a busy pizza shop, deli, family restaurant, or takeout counter, lunch specials should help your staff move orders fast. They should also work when the phone is busy, because lunch calls often come in all at once.

sections.h2: What lunch specials sell best on the phone?
sections.body:
The best lunch specials are the ones a caller can understand in one sentence. Think in terms of a main item, a side, and a drink or soup. Keep the choice set small so the person answering the phone does not need to explain a long menu.

Good lunch specials ideas restaurant owners can use often include:
- A sandwich or wrap with chips and a drink
- Two slices plus a drink
- A salad with protein and a roll
- A soup and half sandwich combo
- A lunch plate with rice, veg, and a main

The goal is speed. A caller should hear the special and know what to order right away. A simple script helps: "Our lunch special today is a turkey sandwich, chips, and a drink for one price. Would you like it for pickup?" That line saves time and keeps the call moving.

If you run a menu with many choices, use your lunch special to narrow the decision. That is especially useful when your team is short-staffed or the counter is busy. ROAL can read the live menu and take the order from the items you choose to make available, so your phone host can present the special the same way every time.

sections.h2: How do you price a lunch special without cutting too deep?
sections.body:
Price the special so it feels like a deal, but still fits your food cost and labor. Start with a simple example you can swap for your own numbers.

Say your regular sandwich price is $14. If you bundle it with chips and a drink, you might price the lunch special at $16.50 or $17.50, depending on your costs and neighborhood. The point is to make the offer feel faster and better than ordering each item one by one.

Use this quick check:
1. Pick the main item.
2. Add the side and drink you usually sell.
3. Compare the bundle price to the regular à la carte total.
4. Leave room for prep time and packaging.
5. Make the special easy to quote over the phone.

If you want a rough profit check, plug in your own numbers. For example, if the full combo sells for $17 and your food plus packaging costs are $6, you have $11 left before labor and overhead. Your numbers may be different, but that is the kind of math to do before putting the special on your board.

This matters even more when you compare channels. Delivery apps commonly take a large commission, while phone orders can keep more of the sale inside your restaurant. For a simple comparison, see [phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps) and [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans).

sections.h2: What should you say when someone calls for lunch?
sections.body:
A clear phone script makes lunch specials easier to sell. It also helps staff avoid long pauses and forgotten details.

Try a short flow like this:
- Greet the caller.
- Say the lunch special first.
- Ask if they want pickup or delivery.
- Confirm the item, sides, and drink.
- Give the ready time.
- Repeat the order back.

Example script line: "Today’s lunch special is the chicken cutlet hero with fries and a drink. Would you like that for pickup?"

If the caller asks for changes, keep the language plain: "You can swap the fries for soup for a small add-on." Or: "That item is sold out right now, but I can offer the grilled chicken wrap instead." That last line matters because your phone host should not promise items that are not available.

For restaurants using ROAL, the host can take items, modifiers, notes, name, phone number, and ready time, then send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It can also speak the caller’s language and hand off allergy-sensitive or manager-level calls to staff with a summary. That keeps the lunch line moving without making the call sound robotic.

sections.h2: Which lunch specials work best for different restaurant types?
sections.body:
The right lunch special depends on what you already make well at noon. You do not need a brand-new menu. You need a tight offer that fits your kitchen.

Use this quick matching table:

| Restaurant type | Lunch special idea | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pizza shop | Two slices, drink, and a side | Fast to quote and fast to make |
| Deli | Sandwich, chips, and drink | Easy phone order, easy pickup |
| Family restaurant | Meatloaf, mashed potatoes, and veg | Familiar and filling |
| Burger spot | Burger, fries, and drink | Simple combo people know |
| Italian spot | Pasta with salad or garlic bread | Good value at lunch |
| Thai or Chinese takeout | Lunch entrée with rice | Standard lunch format |

A lunch special should also fit your prep. If a dish slows down the line, keep it off the special board. Lunch is not the time to create extra steps for the kitchen.

One more practical tip: make your special visible in the same places people already check. That can be your website menu, your public menu pages, and your phone greeting. If callers ask about hours, parking, or ingredients, the same host can answer those questions too. ROAL reads public menu pages and can be set up from your website, Google Maps link, or a simple name and city at /try.

sections.h2: How do you make lunch calls shorter and easier to handle?
sections.body:
Lunch specials work best when the call itself is short. That means fewer choices, fewer clarifying questions, and fewer mistakes.

Use this checklist for a fast lunch call:
- Put the special at the top of your menu.
- Use one name for each special.
- Keep modifiers limited.
- Use simple side options.
- Quote the ready time right away.
- Repeat the total order back once.

A practical example: if your special is a $15 chicken parm hero with fries, the caller should not need to choose from six bread types and four sauces. Keep it to the basics unless the guest asks.

This is where call handling matters. Many restaurants miss good lunch orders because the phone is busy during the same 30 minutes every day. You can send calls to your host when you are tied up, or only when the line is unanswered or busy. On many carriers and phone systems, forwarding has its own setup steps, so confirm the exact code or portal with your carrier and test it with a call. For carrier-specific forwarding codes, keep [this phone setup reference](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) handy.

If your staff still answers live, give them one simple rule: do not improvise long explanations. Just state the special, take the order, and move on.

sections.h2: How do you test lunch specials before you print them everywhere?
sections.body:
Test one special at a time before you turn it into a sign, a post, and a menu rewrite. Start with a weekday lunch item that your kitchen can make consistently.

Try this simple test plan:
1. Pick one lunch special.
2. Run it for a week.
3. Watch how often callers ask for it.
4. Note any kitchen bottlenecks.
5. Adjust the price, portion, or sides.

Use ROAL’s dashboard to review call history, transcripts, and kitchen tickets. If callers keep asking the same question, add that answer to your FAQs. If the special needs a clearer name, change the wording in the menu editor. That is much easier than reprinting a full menu every time.

A good test example: say you launch a $16 lunch chicken wrap special. If callers keep asking whether chips are included, then the offer is not clear enough. Rename it to "Chicken wrap, chips, and drink" so there is no confusion.

You can also use small upsells. A caller who orders a sandwich may also want soup, a drink, or a cookie. Keep those upsells light and relevant. If you want ideas for menu structure, see [menu engineering for small restaurants](/blog/menu-engineering-small-restaurant). The goal is not more choices. It is better choices.

sections.h2: What should you do this week to get more lunch takeout calls?
sections.body:
Pick one lunch special, make it easy to say out loud, and put it where callers can hear it fast. Then make sure the phone path is just as simple as the menu.

A practical weekly checklist:
- Choose one weekday lunch combo.
- Write a one-line phone script.
- Put the special on your website and printed menu.
- Tell staff the exact price and ready time.
- Decide when calls should forward during lunch rush.
- Review the first calls and tighten the wording.

takeaways: Keep lunch specials short, familiar, and easy to quote on the phone.
Price bundles with your own food cost in mind, not by copying a competitor.
Use one clear script so staff can move calls faster at noon.
Review call questions and adjust the special name if callers keep asking the same thing.
Make sure forwarding and order taking are simple before lunch rush starts.

faq.q: What are the best lunch specials ideas for a restaurant?
faq.a: The best lunch specials are simple combos people already understand: sandwich and drink, slices and a drink, soup and half sandwich, or a lunch plate. They should be fast to make, easy to repeat back, and easy for callers to order without a long explanation. Keep the choice set small so lunch calls move quickly.

faq.q: How do I price a lunch special for takeout?
faq.a: Start with your regular item price, then add the side, drink, and packaging you plan to include. Compare that total to the bundle price and leave room for prep and labor. Use your own numbers; a special should feel like a deal without turning into a money loser.

faq.q: Should I put lunch specials on my phone greeting?
faq.a: Yes, if you want callers to hear them fast. A one-line greeting like "Today’s lunch special is chicken parm with fries and a drink" can help people order sooner. Keep it short, because the main goal is to get to the order, not to recite the whole menu.
